question: A company centralizes security tooling in a dedicated 'Security' account within AWS Organizations. They want GuardDuty, Security Hub, and IAM Access Analyzer findings from all 50 member accounts to automatically aggregate into the Security account, without requiring each member account to manually enable or configure anything. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Manually enable GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Access Analyzer in each of the 50 accounts and configure each to send findings via a custom EventBridge rule to the Security account's event bus.
options.B: Register the Security account as the delegated administrator for GuardDuty, Security Hub, and IAM Access Analyzer using AWS Organizations integration, then enable organization-wide auto-enroll for new and existing accounts from the Security account.
options.C: Use AWS Control Tower exclusively, since it is the only service capable of delegated administration for security services.
options.D: Create a cross-account IAM role in each of the 50 accounts that the Security account assumes on a schedule to pull findings via the GetFindings API. DESIGN HIGH-PERFORMING ARCHITECTURES

question: A company runs a monolithic ECS service that needs to be decomposed into three microservices, each requiring different scaling characteristics, different IAM permissions, and independent deployment cadences, while all remaining reachable through a single public domain with path-based routing (/orders/*, /inventory/*, /users/*). Which architecture best satisfies these requirements?

options.A: One ECS service running all three microservices as separate containers in the same task definition, fronted by a single ALB target group.
options.B: Three separate ECS services, each with its own task definition, task IAM role, and Application Auto Scaling target, registered as separate target groups behind a single Application Load Balancer using path-based listener rules to route /orders/*, /inventory/*, and /users/* to the appropriate target group.
options.C: Three separate ECS clusters, each with its own Network Load Balancer, and a Route 53 hosted zone with three separate subdomains.
options.D: A single ECS service with three containers in one task definition, each on a different container port, using an NLB with port-based routing. DESIGN RESILIENT ARCHITECTURES AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) — Practice Exam Page 7 of 101

Which architecture best satisfies these requirements? ✗ A. One ECS service running all three microservices as separate containers in the same task definition, fronted by a single ALB target group. ✓ B. Three separate ECS services, each with its own task definition, task IAM role, and Application Auto Scaling target, registered as separate target groups behind a single Application Load Balancer using path-based listener rules to route /orders/*, /inventory/*, and /users/* to the appropriate target group. ✗ C. Three separate ECS clusters, each with its own Network Load Balancer, and a Route 53 hosted zone with three separate subdomains. ✗ D. A single ECS service with three containers in one task definition, each on a different container port, using an NLB with port-based routing. Explanation: Separate ECS services (B) is the correct decomposition boundary because each microservice needs independent scaling policies, independent task IAM roles (least privilege per service), and independent deployment cadence (rolling updates to one service must not redeploy the others) — all of which are properties of the ECS *service* construct, not achievable by co-locating containers in a single task definition. A single ALB with path-based listener rules routing to per-service target groups satisfies the single-public-domain requirement while keeping routing logic in a managed layer-7 load balancer that understands HTTP paths. Option A fails every core requirement: containers in the same task definition scale together (can't scale independently), share one task IAM role (can't apply least privilege per service), and redeploying the task redeploys all three services together (no independent deployment cadence). Option C works functionally but is significantly over-provisioned and more expensive/operationally complex than necessary — three clusters and three NLBs plus subdomain-based routing don't map naturally to the stated requirement of a *single* public domain with *path*-based routing, and NLBs operate at L4 so they cannot natively perform path-based HTTP routing at all. Option D repeats A's coupling problem and additionally misapplies NLB (L4, port-based) for what is explicitly a path-based (L7) routing requirement, which NLB cannot do. question: A three-tier application spans two Availability Zones. During a recent AZ impairment, the application became fully unavailable even though Multi-AZ RDS failed over successfully within 90 seconds. Investigation shows the private subnet's NAT Gateway was in the impaired AZ, and the ALB only had targets registered from that AZ's Auto Scaling group at the time of impairment. Which two architectural changes would prevent a recurrence?

options.A: Deploy a NAT Gateway in each AZ used by the private subnets, and configure each AZ's route table to use the NAT Gateway local to that AZ.
options.B: Configure the Auto Scaling group to span all AZs used by the application (minimum 2, ideally 3) with the ALB registering targets across all of them, so capacity in a healthy AZ can continue serving traffic during an impairment.
options.C: Increase the RDS failover timeout so the database has more time to recover before the application tier gives up.
options.D: Move the NAT Gateway to a public subnet in the same AZ as the majority of application traffic to reduce latency.
options.E: Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer, since NLBs are inherently more available than ALBs during AZ impairments. DESIGN COST-OPTIMIZED ARCHITECTURES

question: A media analytics team queries Parquet-format clickstream logs stored in S3 using Amazon Athena. Monthly Athena costs have grown significantly as data volume increased, even though most queries only need the last 30 days of data and filter on a handful of columns. What is the most effective way to reduce Athena query costs, since Athena bills per byte scanned?

options.A: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the bucket so infrequently queried data automatically moves to cheaper storage classes.
options.B: Partition the data in S3 by date (e.g., year/month/day prefixes) so date-range queries only scan relevant partitions, and ensure the data remains in a columnar format like Parquet so column-pruning avoids scanning unused columns; use a Glue Crawler or CTAS to maintain the partitioned/converted table.
options.C: Increase the Athena workgroup's query result reuse TTL to the maximum allowed value.
options.D: Migrate from Athena to Amazon Redshift Serverless, since Redshift always costs less than Athena for equivalent query volume. DESIGN SECURE ARCHITECTURES AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) — Practice Exam Page 8 of 101

question: An application running on EC2 instances in a private subnet needs to call the Amazon S3 API. The security team mandates that instances must never have a route to the public internet, not even through a NAT Gateway, but S3 access must still work. Additionally, the S3 bucket policy must ensure requests can only originate from within a specific VPC, rejecting any request that somehow reaches the bucket via the public internet from that VPC's credentials. What combination of controls satisfies both requirements?

options.A: Attach an internet gateway to the VPC and use security groups to block all internet-bound traffic except to S3's public IP ranges.
options.B: Create a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 in the route table used by the private subnet (providing connectivity with no internet path), and add a bucket policy condition using aws:SourceVpce (or aws:SourceVpc) that denies access unless the request came through that specific VPC endpoint.
options.C: Create an Interface VPC Endpoint (PrivateLink) for S3 and rely on the endpoint's default security group to restrict access; no bucket policy changes are needed since PrivateLink is inherently private.
options.D: Use AWS PrivateLink with a NAT Gateway fallback for redundancy, and restrict access using an S3 ACL granting access only to the VPC's CIDR range. DESIGN RESILIENT ARCHITECTURES

What combination of controls satisfies both requirements? ✗ A. Attach an internet gateway to the VPC and use security groups to block all internet-bound traffic except to S3's public IP ranges. ✓ B. Explanation: A Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 provides private connectivity to S3 entirely within the AWS network via route table entries — no internet gateway, no NAT Gateway, and no public IP path is involved at all, satisfying the 'never a route to the public internet' requirement precisely. Option C incorrectly describes Interface Endpoints as 'inherently private' in a way that removes the need for a bucket policy — without the aws:SourceVpce condition, credentials used from outside the VPC could still successfully call S3 over the public internet, so the second requirement (rejecting non-VPC-origin requests) would not be met; a security group on the endpoint also controls network reachability to the endpoint, not S3 API-level authorization. question: A company runs a critical order-processing workflow: API Gateway receives orders, a Lambda function validates them, and a second Lambda function writes to Aurora and calls a third-party payment API that occasionally has 30+ second outages. Under load, validation Lambdas frequently time out waiting on the payment-calling Lambda, and failed orders are silently lost with no retry. Which redesign most improves resilience and decouples the components properly?

options.B: Have the validation Lambda publish validated orders to an SQS standard queue with a dead-letter queue configured; a separate Lambda consumes from the queue to call the payment API and write to Aurora, with SQS's built-in visibility timeout and redrive policy handling retries and isolating failures.
options.C: Combine both Lambda functions into a single function to eliminate the inter-function dependency entirely.
options.D: Use Step Functions Express Workflows with a synchronous Lambda invocation chain and no error handling, since Express Workflows are optimized for high-volume, short-duration workloads. question: A data analytics platform runs Spark jobs on Amazon EMR that require extremely high, sustained sequential-read throughput from shared storage across hundreds of nodes, with data seeded from S3 at job start and results written back to S3 at job end. Which two storage choices are most appropriate for the EMR cluster's working/scratch storage during job execution?

options.A: Amazon FSx for Lustre, linked to the source S3 bucket, providing a high-throughput, POSIX-compliant, scale-out parallel file system optimized for HPC/big-data workloads with sub-millisecond latencies.
options.B: Amazon EFS in General Purpose performance mode, since EFS scales automatically and requires no capacity planning.
options.C: Instance store (NVMe SSD) volumes on compute-optimized or storage-optimized EC2 instance types for HDFS scratch space local to each node, sized appropriately for the working dataset.
options.D: A single large gp3 EBS volume shared across all nodes via EBS Multi-Attach for centralized scratch storage.
options.E: Amazon S3 Standard as the sole scratch storage layer accessed directly via EMRFS for every intermediate shuffle write, avoiding any local or networked scratch storage entirely. DESIGN SECURE ARCHITECTURES

Amazon FSx for Lustre, linked to the source S3 bucket, providing a high-throughput, POSIX-compliant, scale-out parallel file system optimized for HPC/big-data workloads with sub-millisecond latencies. ✗ B. question: A company's on-premises data center connects to AWS via a single AWS Direct Connect connection to support a hybrid workload with strict low-latency requirements. Leadership is concerned about the Direct Connect connection itself becoming a single point of failure, whether due to a fiber cut, a device failure at the Direct Connect location, or an issue within that specific AWS Direct Connect location entirely. Which two design changes address these distinct failure modes appropriately?

options.A: Provision a second Direct Connect connection at a different Direct Connect location (ideally via a different network provider/path) to protect against a fiber cut or device failure, following AWS's documented resiliency model for 'High Resiliency' or 'Maximum Resiliency.'
options.B: Configure a Site-to-Site VPN connection as a backup path over the public internet, with BGP configured so it is automatically preferred as a failover route if the Direct Connect path becomes unavailable.
options.C: Increase the bandwidth of the existing single Direct Connect connection, since higher bandwidth reduces the likelihood of failure.
options.D: Enable Direct Connect SiteLink on the existing single connection, since SiteLink alone provides redundancy across Direct Connect locations.
options.E: Rely solely on Direct Connect's default 99.9% SLA, since AWS automatically reroutes traffic during any single connection failure with no customer-side configuration required. question: A company runs an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster supporting an internal analytics tool used heavily during business hours (9am–6pm on weekdays) and almost not at all outside those hours or on weekends. Current sizing uses a fixed pair of db.r6g.xlarge instances running continuously. Leadership wants to reduce cost while maintaining performance during business hours without manual intervention. What is the best approach?

options.A: Migrate to Aurora Serverless v2, which scales database capacity (in ACUs) automatically and near-instantly based on actual load, billing per ACU-second, so capacity (and cost) shrinks automatically during nights/weekends and scales up during business hours without manual scheduling.
options.B: Purchase a 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instance for the db.r6g.xlarge instances to lock in the lowest possible hourly rate, since the workload runs continuously regardless of utilization.
options.C: Manually resize the instances to a smaller instance class every evening and resize back up every morning using a person on-call.
options.D: Move the analytics tool to run entirely within Redshift Serverless instead of Aurora, since Redshift is always cheaper for analytics workloads regardless of usage pattern. DESIGN HIGH-PERFORMING ARCHITECTURES

question: An application uses ElastiCache for Redis as a session store for a web tier running across multiple AZs. The current single-node Redis deployment recently failed, causing every logged-in user to be logged out simultaneously, which is unacceptable. The team wants automatic failover with minimal data loss and continued read/write availability during a node failure. What ElastiCache for Redis configuration should be used?

options.A: Redis (cluster mode disabled) with Multi-AZ enabled and at least one read replica, so ElastiCache automatically promotes a replica to primary and updates the DNS endpoint on primary node failure, providing automatic failover.
options.B: A single larger Redis node with more memory, since vertical scaling alone prevents node failures.
options.C: Memcached with multiple nodes, since Memcached natively supports automatic failover and data replication across nodes.
options.D: Redis cluster mode disabled with no replicas, but with daily automated backups, since backups are sufficient to restore session data on failure. DESIGN SECURE ARCHITECTURES AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) — Practice Exam Page 16 of 101

explanation: Single n application uses ElastiCache for Redis as a session store for a web tier running across multiple AZs. The current single-node Redis deployment recently failed, causing every logged-in user to be logged out simultaneously, which is unacceptable. The team wants automatic failover with minimal data loss and continued read/write availability during a node failure. What ElastiCache for Redis configuration should be used? ✓ A. Redis (cluster mode disabled) with Multi-AZ enabled and at least one read replica, so ElastiCache automatically promotes a replica to primary and updates the DNS endpoint on primary node failure, providing automatic failover. ✗ B. A single larger Redis node with more memory, since vertical scaling alone prevents node failures. ✗ C. Memcached with multiple nodes, since Memcached natively supports automatic failover and data replication across nodes. ✗ D. Redis cluster mode disabled with no replicas, but with daily automated backups, since backups are sufficient to restore session data on failure. Explanation: ElastiCache for Redis with Multi-AZ enabled and at least one replica (A) directly solves the described failure mode: Redis replication continuously copies data from primary to replica(s), and when Multi-AZ is enabled, ElastiCache automatically detects primary node failure and promotes a replica (ideally in a different AZ) to become the new primary, updating the cluster's endpoint automatically — typically within about a minute, this preserves the vast majority of session data (near-real-time replication) and restores read/write availability without requiring the application to reconnect to a new hostname manually, since the endpoint remains stable. Option B does not address the actual problem — a bigger single node is still a single point of failure; vertical scaling improves capacity/performance, not availability, and the node can still fail for reasons unrelated to size (AZ impairment, hardware fault, etc.). Option C is factually incorrect: Memcached is explicitly a non-replicating, in-memory cache with no built-in data replication or automatic failover between nodes — it's designed as a simple, horizontally-partitioned cache, not a durable or highly available session store, making it a worse fit than Redis for this exact requirement. Option D (backups only, no replica) means that during the outage itself, there is no available Redis endpoint to serve reads/writes at all until a new node is manually or automatically provisioned and restored from backup, which involves real downtime measured in minutes and loses all session data written since the last backup — it does not provide continued availability during the failure, only eventual recovery, which fails the 'minimal data loss and continued availability' requirement.
